title: Live a hundred years, working
hookLine: a cobbler stays at his bench, and the river reaches out to him
carry: work offered to god doesn't bind

cards: In Varanasi, some five or six hundred years ago, lived Ravidas: a leatherworker who mended shoes, and a poet-saint whose songs are still sung, and are also in the Sikh scripture.
A well-loved story says his neighbors set off for a festival bath in the Ganga and asked him to come. Ravidas had shoes promised to a customer that day.
So he stayed at his bench and handed them a coin: offer this to Mother Ganga for me, but only if she reaches out to take it. At the river, the story says, a hand rose out of the water and took it.

teach.h: THE GANGA IN MY WORK BOWL.
teach.b: Ravidas is remembered for a saying that grew around it: man changa to kathauti mein Ganga. If the mind is pure, the Ganga is right here in my work bowl. That's the Isha's second verse, lived.

teach.h: DOING WORKS HERE, LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.
teach.b: Kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah: doing your works here, wish to live a hundred years. Karmani is works, the same karma you met on day seven. A hundred years is the full life the old Vedic prayers ask for.
Then the reason: for you, living this way, action does not cling. The word pictures something smeared on, like oil. Work done knowing all this is the Lord's doesn't glue itself to you.
This is the root of karma yoga, the Gita's path you spent weeks with: act fully, offer the work, let go of the fruit.
And it's why Hinduism honors the householder, the grihastha, who works, raises a family and feeds people, as a real road to God, not a lesser one. You can see it in Hindu life.

Once a year, at Ayudha Puja or Vishwakarma Puja, many workshops and homes honor their tools: the sewing machine, the laptop, the truck get kumkum and a flower. Elders bless the young: may you live a hundred years.
And plenty of grandmothers will tell you their cooking is their puja. Ravidas didn't need to leave his bench to reach the river.
Offered rightly, the work was the river.

how: Hindu teachers often cite Isha verse 2 to show the Upanishads do not require leaving the world; many Hindus honor their tools at Ayudha Puja or Vishwakarma Puja and offer their daily work to God.

o: a punishment sent for past mistakes
action, the works a person does
fate that's fixed before you're born

games.q: verses two and three — tap the pairs.
p: the cobbler-saint who stayed at his bench

s: the Isha tells everyone to quit their work and withdraw
verse two says doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years.
in the story, Ravidas left his shoes to bathe in the Ganga
he stayed with the work he'd promised; the story says the river reached for his coin.
Isha verse two holds the seed of the Gita's karma yoga
act fully, and the action doesn't cling to you.

games.q: once a year a family puts kumkum and a flower on the laptop and the delivery truck. what's the teaching?
o: it's a trick for better sales.
work offered to the Lord is worship, and it doesn't bind you.
tools are gods, so you shouldn't use them.
games.why: Ayudha Puja and Vishwakarma Puja honor the work itself. Isha verse two: done this way, action does not cling.

practice: Pick one task waiting for you today: the dishes, a report, a practice session. Before you start, offer it. If you pray, say silently, this is for you, or touch the tool to your forehead, the way many Hindus honor their tools.
If you don't pray, dedicate it to someone you love. Then do it well, and when it's done, let it go, like washing oil off your hands.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, works. Verse two: doing works here, wish to live a hundred years; action done this way, offered, doesn't cling.

orig.note: Sanskrit: karma, action; verse two uses karmani, works, from the root kri, to do.

carryVoice: Your line: work offered to god doesn't bind. Ravidas stayed at his bench, and the river came to him. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 2 (doing works, live a hundred years; action does not cling)
Ravidas hagiographic tradition (the coin for the Ganga; the saying 'man changa to kathauti mein Ganga')
